source.title: Can SAEs reveal and mitigate racial biases of LLMs in healthcare?

record.file_problem: none; full paper text is present.
record.tranche_reason: The study tests SAE latents for racial associations and bias interventions in healthcare, not whether neuron poles have one or two main jobs, whether neuron explanations generalize to held-out activations, or whether neuron-based attribution graphs suffice. Its SAE results are related to internal-feature interpretability but do not test any listed claim version.
record.gate_note: The paper reports results on SAE latents, their steering and ablation, and model outputs; these are recorded as related findings under versions ["none"]. It does not report a neuron-pole audit, held-out testing of neuron explanations, an InceptionV1 analysis, or neuron-based attribution graphs. The clinical task racial-bias results before intervention (Table 6) are not recorded as rows because they measure race effects, not the claimed neuron interpretability properties. Results cited from other work are excluded.
record.test_reason: The study probes, steers and ablates Gemma Scope SAE latents (not model neurons) to detect and mitigate racial bias in clinical tasks. It reports no neuron-pole audit, no shares of one-job or two-job neurons, no InceptionV1 analysis, no neuron-based attribution graphs and no held-out or simulation scoring of neuron explanations. It relies on SAEs and an automated-interpretability pipeline as tools without measuring neuron interpretability. So it neither tests nor uses the claim; the record's 'discusses' overstates the link, since the paper never engages the neurons-are-clean thesis.
record.authors_conclusion: Correct. SAEs can reveal problematic race associations and steering shows a causal effect that CoT does not reveal. Ablation reduces bias in contrived vignette generation but is minimally effective on realistic clinical tasks, where race may be entangled with clinical concepts.
record.recipe_differences: The study uses Gemma 2 SAE latents, race probes, steering, and ablation in healthcare tasks. It does not perform the original neuron-pole audit or test neuron explanations as described in the claim.
record.method_sensitivity: The paper reports different SAE layers for the 2B and 9B models; steering factors vary by model and target race. It reports no significant improvement from ablating race latents in five layers rather than the middle layer.

fits_no_version.finding: Neuronpedia descriptions of Gemma Scope SAE latents were sometimes wrong or imprecise in clinical text. For example, latent 14880 is labelled vehicle maintenance but fires on surgical valve replacements. Re-explaining latents on domain text gave more relevant descriptions (Table 1, qualitative).
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Activating-example explanations of SAE latents derived on general text can mislead in a new domain, so descriptions should be domain-specific.

fits_no_version.finding: The Black SAE latent fires on Black identity mentions and also on incarceration, gunshot wounds and cocaine use (Figure 1; similar in gpt-oss-20b).
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Race-predictive SAE latents in Gemma 2 mix identity references with stigmatizing clinical concepts.

record.problems: The authors analyze racial bias only in Gemma 2 models for their main experiments, use datasets from the same hospital, and focus on Black and white patients. They describe vignette generation as a contrived setting and say SAE mitigation is less reliable on realistic clinical tasks. Most row-level results have no reported uncertainty; statistical significance is reported for the separate pre-intervention racial-bias tests.
record.rows_left_out: No rows omitted for the 60-row limit. Table 6's pre-intervention race-bias measurements and the text-only prompt-versus-SAE effects in Section 4.2 are not included because they do not measure the claimed neuron interpretability properties or a listed version.

untested.parts: No audit of neuron poles in Qwen3-32B or any model.
No neuron-share comparison across models or scale; gpt-oss-20b is used only for a qualitative SAE latent example.
No test of architecture or tool effects on interpretable neuron share.
No test of neuron explanations against held-out firing.
No simulation scoring of neuron explanations; the detection scores for SAE latent descriptions are not reported.

record.verdict_notes: All rows correctly carry versions ['none']. The objects studied are SAE latents, not neurons, so even the latent-description reinterpretation finding is outside V6 and V7, which name neuron explanations. The detection-metric scores for the reinterpreted descriptions are computed but never reported. Relation changed to cites_only because the paper does not discuss the claim.

versions.untested_parts: No audit of neuron poles or proportions of single-job, two-job, or not-understood poles.
No comparison of neuron-pole shares across model families, architectures, or scales.
No InceptionV1 cat-and-car neuron or recursive-generalization analysis.
No test of architecture, regularization, tool quality, or changing interpretability shares.
No attribution graphs built from model neurons and no comparison with a trained replacement model or reconstruction error.
No test of explanations written from activating examples against where a neuron fires on other examples.
No evaluation of neuron explanations by simulating neuron activations on new text.

rows.subject: gemma-2-2B-it
rows.operation_detail: A logistic-regression probe used max-aggregated SAE latent activations to predict patient race; AUROC reported for the top Black latent.
rows.measure: AUROC for race prediction from the single latent's max-aggregated activations
rows.note: The paper says race was mentioned in only 4.3% of notes; this is a latent-level result, not a neuron-pole audit.
